title: What is a high yield savings account?
summary: A high yield savings account pays more interest than a standard savings account. Learn how it works, what to compare, and if it fits your goals.
body_markdown:
You deposit money, and the bank pays you interest (a percentage of your balance) for keeping it there. The difference is the rate.


A high yield account pays more than the national average for standard savings accounts.


The rate is usually shown as APY, or annual percentage yield. APY is the total you earn in one year, including compound interest (interest paid on your earlier interest).


It is different from APR, or annual percentage rate, which is the term most often used for loans.


Many online banks can offer higher rates because they don't run large branch networks. Those savings can go back to customers as interest. You can still deposit, withdraw, and transfer money through an app or website.


Most of these accounts have a variable rate, which means the bank can raise or lower it over time. Deposits are typically insured by the FDIC (Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation) up to the standard limit.


Both account types are built for money you want to keep safe and within reach. The main gap is how much interest they pay and how they are offered.

If you want a deeper look at how yield is calculated, read our guide on[what is APY](https://www.axosbank.com/personal/insights/finance/digital-banking/what-is-apy) .


These accounts suit many savers, but they are not perfect for everyone. Here is the upside:


-


**Earn more interest:** Your balance grows faster than it would in a standard account.


-


**Keep easy access:** You can usually move money in and out without penalties.


-


**Get deposit protection:** Accounts at FDIC-insured banks are protected up to the legal limit.


And here are the trade-offs to weigh:


-


**Rates can change:** A variable rate may drop when the broader interest rate environment shifts.


-


**Terms may apply:** Some banks set minimum balances, charge fees, or limit monthly withdrawals.


-


**Interest is taxable:** Interest you earn generally counts as income at tax time.


Terms vary by bank, and a financial advisor or tax professional can help you decide what fits your situation.


Not every account labeled "high yield" is the same. A few checks make comparing options easier:


-


**Compare the APY:** Look at the current APY, and ask whether the bank has a history of keeping its rate competitive.


-


**Check fees and minimums:** A monthly fee or a high minimum balance can cancel out the extra interest.


-


**Confirm FDIC insurance:** Make sure the bank is FDIC-insured so your deposits are protected.


-


**Review access options:** Look for an app, online transfers, and linked checking so moving money stays simple.


-


**Think about your goal:** An emergency fund needs quick access, while a short-term goal like a vacation may let you save automatically each month.

A high yield savings account gives you the safety and access of a regular savings account with a better chance to grow your money. It works well for emergency funds and short-term goals.

### **Is a high yield savings account worth it?**


For most savers, yes, because it earns more than a standard account with similar access. The benefit is biggest on larger balances held for longer periods.


### **Is a high yield savings account safe?**


It is as safe as any deposit account when held at an FDIC-insured bank. Deposits are covered up to the standard limit.


### **How often do high yield savings account rates change?**


Rates are variable, so banks can change them at any time. Many follow moves in the broader interest rate environment.


### **Is the interest from a high yield savings account taxable?**


In general, yes. Interest is usually treated as income for the year you earn it. A tax professional can explain how it applies to you.
